citeinfo.othercit: Breitmeyer, S.E., Hinman, E.D., Sleckman, M.J., and Shoda, M.E., 2026, Riverine Surface Water Pesticide Concentrations, Detection Frequencies, Benchmark Exceedances, and Trends for the Conterminous United States, 2013-2022: U.S. Geological Survey data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/P1NDXVYD.

descript.abstract:
The data tables in this product include concentrations, detection frequencies, benchmark exceedances, and trends of pesticides in riverine surface water samples. The data are a product of a national-scale assessment of the status and trends of 84 pesticides at 81 sites during water years 2013 - 2022 conducted by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) National Water Quality Program.
Data were collected to: 1) determine where and how often pesticides are detected in riverine surface waters, 2) quantify where, when, and how often riverine pesticide concentrations exceed both aquatic-life and human-health benchmarks, and 3) assess if trends in concentrations of individual pesticides can be detected over the decade of water years 2013 – 2022, and if the magnitude and direction of the trend can be determined.
descript.purpose: These data were retrieved and processed for use in benchmark exceedance and trend assessments of surface water pesticide concentrations in USGS National Water Quality Network of rivers and streams.
descript.supplinf:
To open the text file tables in Excel so that leading or trailing zeroes are not deleted from values in the USGS site number (in tables 1 through 7), state code (table 1), hydrologic unit code (in table 1), percentage data (tables 3 and 7), concentration data (tables 2 through 7), and statistical result (table 7) columns: 1. Open Excel and click on the **File** tab. 2. Click on the **Open** button and then click on the **Browse** button. 3. Navigate to the location of the text file that you want to open. 4. Select the text file and then click on the **Open** button. 5. The Text Import Wizard will appear. 6. In the **Text Import Wizard**, click on the **Next** button for steps 1 and 2. 7. In the **Column Data Format** section, select the **Text** option for each desired column where leading or trailing zeroes need to be retained. 8. Click on the **Next** button. 9. Click on the **Finish** button.
If using a programming language to open the data tables it is suggested to read in the compressed parquet files, rather than the text files, of each data table so that leading or trailing zeroes are not deleted from values in the USGS site number (in tables 1 through 7), state code (table 1), hydrologic unit code (in table 1), percentage data (tables 3 and 7), concentration data (tables 2 through 7), and statistical result (table 7) columns. If using a programming language to open the data tables and the preferred method is to read in the text files of the data table, all columns should be read in as character classes (i.e., string or object types) to retain any leading and trailing zeroes in each column.

procstep.procdesc:
Site information
Site information data, with the exception of region and aggregated region, were queried using the R dataRetrieval package (DeCicco and others, 2024). Aggregated region and region variables were from Martinez and others (2025). Two sites (Wax Lake Outlet at Calumet, LA and Lower Atchafalaya River at Morgan City, LA) were classified as distributaries (streams that branch off and flow away from the main river channel) and thus, no upstream drainage areas were defined for these sites. Sacramento River at Freeport, CA had no upstream drainage area available when site information was queried from the R dataRetrieval package (DeCicco and others, 2024), so the respective drainage area was from Stackpoole and others (2021).
The two Illinois River sites (Illinois River at Valley City, IL and Illinois River at Florence, IL) were combined and processed as one site for all pesticide quality control steps and analyses and hence, this site is represented by one abbreviated site name (Illinois R, IL) throughout data release tables 2 through 7. These two sites were combined because they represent the same river reach and had a change of National Water Quality Network sampling location, from Illinois River at Valley City, IL to the Illinois River at Florence, IL, during the period of record (POR). Hence, pesticide samples that were collected from the Illinois River at Valley City, IL from water years 2013 through 2018 were combined with pesticide samples collected from the Illinois River at Florence, IL from water years 2015 through 2022 for QC processing steps and benchmark comparison, trend, and time-weighted detection frequency analyses.

Pesticide concentration quality control (QC), and other data screening
A complete description of the USGS National Water Quality Laboratory (NWQL) 2437 and 2447 Pesticide Schedule Method including information about 1) sample collection and handling procedures, 2) description of the analysis by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry, and 3) quality assurance and quality control is outlined in Sandstrom and others (2015) and Shoda and others (2018) and the Supplemental Information associated with those publications. The NWQL switched from Pesticide Schedule 2437 to 2447 in 2018. Although both schedules use the same analytical methodology (liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry), the number of pesticides analyzed were reduced in the 2447 schedule.
Pesticide concentration data were retrieved from the USGS National Water Information System (NWIS) database (U.S. Geological Survey, 2024) for water years 2013 through 2022 using the USGS site numbers and pesticide parameter codes. The analytical method for determining pesticide concentrations has a different level of resolution for each pesticide, which is determined by the chemical properties of the compounds, and thus reporting levels (RLs) for this method range from 0.00200 to 48.0 microgram L-1, with an RL of <0.0400 microgram L-1 for roughly 75% of the pesticides. The method detection level (MDL) = (0.5*the stated reporting level (RL)).
Data processing involved multiple steps, each of which is documented in the companion USGS software release, Hinman and others (2025). For example, screening of observations included quality control screening such as reviewing the concentration results for the presence of values of zero, checking for the presence of duplicate results, and reviewing NWQL provided value qualifier codes. Data processing also included screening for raised reporting levels. A raised reporting level (RRL) is a "Not Detected" value reported at a concentration higher than the RL associated with the sample result. RRLs were screened according to the following steps: (1) removal from the dataset due to contamination or undefined reasons for occurrence, (2) when greater than or equal to 90 percent of the results for a pesticide were non-detections, all RRLs were retained, (3) the remaining RRLs were categorized as “quantized” or “non-quantized” following Hinman and others (2025), (4) quantized RRLs greater than the 50th percentile of detected values were removed, and (5) non-quantized RRLs greater than the 25th percentile of detected values were removed. Screening of each site-pesticide's longitudinal data for representativeness and completeness was also conducted following Stone and others (2014).

Time-weighted detection frequencies
To provide an unbiased estimate of the percentage of time during the water year that a compound was detected, time-weighted detection frequencies (DFs) of each pesticide were calculated for 81 sites throughout 10 water years (2013-2022) following methods described in Stone and others (2014). Time-weighted annual means are also provided, where “Not Detected” values were set to half of their RL (MDL) in the calculation. Further details regarding the calculation of time-weighted DFs can be found in the software (code) that was used to generate these data (Hinman and others, 2025).

Acute aquatic life benchmark (ALB) exceedances
Only detected concentrations are included in the acute ALB comparison table. A sample result was considered to have exceeded an acute benchmark for a pesticide if the concentration was greater than or equal to the benchmark. The benchmarks used in this analysis were derived from EPA Office of Pesticide Programs (OPP) aquatic-life benchmarks (EPA, Aquatic Life Benchmarks, 2024). When the EPA did not have an exact equivalent to this study’s analyte list, the appropriate benchmark was selected by evaluating chemically similar compounds. This determination considered factors such as structural similarity, functional groups, and naming variations (e.g., acids versus salts, esters, combined acid/salt forms, or isomers). For detailed information on the pesticide benchmarks applied, see Table 4 (t4_ALB_acute), specifically the “Benchmark_Comment” column. Further details regarding the calculation of acute ALB exceedances can be found in the software (code) that was used to generate these data (Hinman and others, 2025).

Chronic aquatic life benchmark (ALB) exceedances
A site was considered to have exceeded a chronic ALB benchmark for pesticide and water year if the appropriate moving-average concentration was greater than or equal to the benchmark concentration. Moving-average concentrations were calculated as described in Stone and others (2014), and the benchmarks used in this analysis were derived from EPA Office of Pesticide Programs (OPP) aquatic-life benchmarks (EPA, Aquatic Life Benchmarks, 2024). When the EPA did not have an exact equivalent to this study’s analyte list, the appropriate benchmark was selected by evaluating chemically similar compounds. This determination considered factors such as structural similarity, functional groups, and naming variations (e.g., acids versus salts, esters, combined acid/salt forms, or isomers). For detailed information on the pesticide benchmarks applied, see Table 5 (t5_ALB_chronic), specifically the “Benchmark_Comment” column. Further details regarding the calculation of chronic ALB exceedances can be found in the software (code) that was used to generate these data (Hinman and others, 2025).

Human health benchmark exceedances
The EPA Drinking Water Standard Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCL) from Smith and Nowell (2024) were used for the chronic Human Health Benchmark (HHB) comparisons for four pesticides that had an available MCL (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D), atrazine, glyphosate, and simazine). If available, the EPA Human Health Benchmarks for Pesticides (HHBPs) and USGS Health Based Screening Levels (HBSLs) were used for additional chronic benchmark comparisons (Smith and Nowell, 2024). Following guidance from Smith and Nowell (2024), estimated annual mean concentrations were compared to the HHB benchmarks. Annual mean concentrations were estimated based on the percent of non-detections for each pesticide, monitoring location, and water year. If less than 10 percent of results were non-detections, then a time-weighted annual mean was calculated with all non-detections set to the MDL. If greater than 80 percent of results were non-detections, then the most frequent non-detection value was used as the estimated annual mean. If between 10 and 80 percent of results were non-detections, then a Kaplan-Meier median was used to estimate the annual mean, where non-detections were included at their RL. Further details regarding the calculation of HHB exceedances can be found in the software (code) that was used to generate these data (Hinman and others, 2025).

Pesticide trends
Pesticide trends were computed utilizing the EnvStats (Millard, 2013) and NADA2 (Julian and Helsel, 2024) R packages. To determine monotonic changes in pesticide concentrations over time, the Seasonal Kendall Test (SKT) was utilized (Hirsch and others,1982). The SKT uses the Tau statistic, a nonparametric measure of correlative strength ranging from −1 to 1, indicating a stronger negative or positive trend as the Tau value approaches −1 or 1, respectively (Hirsch and others, 1982). The magnitude of change was determined using the Thiel-Sen slope, which is a representation of the median slope of all pairwise comparisons through the data (Julian and Helsel, 2024; Hirsch and others, 1982).
Before running the SKT on pesticide concentrations for the trend period (a single decade-long period, water years 2013−2022), several data screening steps were performed using modified methods from Shoda and Murphy (2022). For each river-pesticide combination, the following criteria were used to assess dataset for suitability in SKT analysis:
1) Outlier: river-pesticide(s) did not contain high outliers (>= 4 standard deviations). 2) Data Density: river-pesticide(s) had at least 20 samples with a minimum 9-year period of record (POR), with quarterly samples for at least 70% of the POR. No data gaps longer than 5 years. 3) Seasonal and temporal: records were defined by a quarterly sampling scheme that is used in multiple national modeling efforts (Division III sampling scenario from Table 4 in Oelsner and others (2017)). The POR was 10 years long. Because 2022 was the target end year, the minimum start year was 2013. a. End-year: at least 2 years of quarterly sampling in a 3-year end-year window (2 preceding years + target year). For this analysis, the target trend end year is 2022 and the end year window is 2020 – 2022. b. Start-year: Quarterly samples were required in the start-year and in at least 1 of the next 3 years (i.e., at least 2 years with quarterly samples were required in the 4-year start window; quarterly samples were required in 2013 and in one of the following years: 2014, 2015, or 2016.
For pesticide and site combinations that had multiple reporting levels, the data were censored to the highest reporting level. In this process, if there was a single result for a given season and year, that value was used. If there were multiple results, then the median value for that season, determined with the flipped Kaplan-Meier method, was used (Millard, 2013).
Estimates of the Theil-Sen slope become unreliable when a large percentage of the water-quality record is censored, while the Tau statistic is more robust to censored data. In this situation, a significant increasing or decreasing trend can be identified, but the magnitude of the trend cannot be reliably quantified. If less than or equal to 40 percent of the seasons were censored, then the Tau statistic and the Theil-Sen slope were reported (Shoda and Murphy, 2022). If more than 40 percent but less than or equal to 80 percent of the seasonal data in the trend period were censored, then only the Tau statistic was reported. Finally, if more than 80 percent of the seasons in the trend period were censored values, the SKT was not run, following Oelsner and others (2017), and only the median Kaplan-Meier concentration of the trend period was reported. Further details regarding the calculation of trends can be found in the software (code) that was used to generate these data (Hinman and others, 2025).
